Lessons.Title: Dive Back Into Division
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 G5 U08:L04 returns to whole-number division with up to four-digit dividend and two-digit divisor, asking first if quotient estimates are REASONABLE then finding exact result and constructing infinitely many valid missing-dividend/divisor expressions.
Warm-up Notice and Wonder Blank Spaces displays blank÷blank=136; source invites many valid pairs and peer reasoning, not one official answer.

Activity1 Reasonable Estimates original364÷13=28 near30 of choices20 30 40, 540÷12=45 exactly halfway between40 and50 (either a defensible estimate if closeness is only criterion),1008÷14=72 nearest70 of70 80 90. The three original exact quotient figures labeled a/b/c are image-only and require teacher review.

Activity2 Missing Dividends and Divisors asks for FIVE different pairs each yielding700 and78; infinite valid possibilities include7000÷10=700,780÷10=78. Teacher verifies variety and method rather than grading one sample as only correct.

Prior first-party728÷24 remains an optional extension. Source estimated versus exact values are separated and static numeric Practice does not claim to score student-generated equations or image-only division work.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: estimate whole-number quotients using friendly multiplication benchmarks and then reason from a given quotient to multiple different valid dividend–divisor pairs. This revisits partial quotients without forcing one calculation strategy.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: a calculator-free quotient estimate for364÷13 can use 13×20=260 and13×30=390; 364 is closer to390 than260 so thirty is a reasonable tens estimate. To compute exactly, remove20 groups of13 leaving104, then eight more groups of13, giving28. Ask learners to explain why different chunk selections are equally legal.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — original estimate cases: 728÷24 is near30 because24×30=720 (exact30 remainder8). For 1008÷14, exact72 and a tens estimate70 is reasonable. In the 2021 source 540÷12=45 with choices 40,50,60 has a TIE between40 and50 by absolute distance; do not auto-mark one unique nearest-ten answer unless the activity provides a further rounding convention. Both are justifiable benchmarks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — make different quotient equations: give a quotient of78 and ask for at least four different valid positive whole-number pairs, such as78÷1,156÷2,390÷5,780÷10. Give a quotient of700 and construct700÷1,1400÷2,3500÷5,7000÷10. A student must produce novel pairs and explain divisor×quotient=dividend, not just copy one template.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Teacher boundary: the source asks pupils to compare reasonable estimates, multiple distinct example equations, group explanations, and a visual gallery. Exact division is supporting Practice, not proof that a strategy or a set of ten genuinely distinct equations was authored.

KeyConcepts.Title: Estimate quotient using multiples
KeyConcepts.Definition: Compare a dividend with friendly positive multiples of divisor before exact partial quotients.

KeyConcepts.Title: Partial quotient flexibility
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different sums of valid divisor group-counts yield same dividend.

KeyConcepts.Title: Families with fixed quotient
KeyConcepts.Definition: For integer quotient q>0 and nonzero integer divisor d>0, dividend qd gives a valid quotient q.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Guess a missing dividend without multiplying quotient by divisor
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A quotient alone does not give a unique dividend.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Choose a nonzero divisor first and calculate dividend=divisor×quotient.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reject one equally close tens estimate in a tie
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Two benchmarks may be equally near an exact quotient.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare absolute distances and state the tie if no convention resolves it.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Replace original printed multi-digit factors and numerical source strategies with fictional practice without attribution.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original IM2021 printed student activities use specific decimal values and require place-value reasoning, so substituting unrelated examples or accepting a right-justified digit alignment does not preserve source parity.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use original exact figures and maintain the visual/teacher review boundary for figure-only computations and open strategy explanations.

Lessons.Title: What’s the Difference?
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 G5 U08:L11 uses unlike-denominator subtraction, adaptive strategic reasoning, and a spinner game with a greatest difference followed by a puzzle to minimize the sum of TWO differences.
Warm-up source2/3−1/6=1/2,2/3−1/2=1/6,2/3−4/6=zero and2/3−1/4=5/12. Student explains why renaming2/3 in sixths or twelfths changes number of pieces but not quantity.

Activity1 Greatest Difference gives students multiple rounds of spinner rolls filling locked fraction numerator and denominator blanks. The GREATEST fraction difference wins; source does not provide any fixed roll sequence or official unique result.

Activity2 What is the Smallest Difference? printed numbers1,1,2,2,3,4,5,6 fill eight boxes making TWO subtraction expressions and student tries to minimize their combined result. This is an optimization under rule constraints, not a single response to unrelated invented fractions.

Previously authored examples remain optional extensions; selected source Practice includes warm-up fractions and fixed rules only, with student-generated subtraction choices and original teacher discussions evaluated by teacher.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: use unlike-denominator fractions in a repeated strategy GAME that seeks the largest difference, then an independent task seeks the SMALLEST total of two differences. The 2021 source's four rounds require recording random spinner digits as they occur; the answer depends on each player's choices and cannot be reduced to one official number.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: compare5/6−1/3=1/2 with5/6−1/4=7/12 and explain how a smaller subtrahend makes the result larger when the minuend stays fixed. Fractions must be renormalized into equal-size pieces before subtracting.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — demonstration rounds: choose digits for the numerator and denominator of two fraction differences using a given bank1,1,2,2,3,4,5,6. An original trial uses6/1−1/5=29/5 and4/2−2/3=4/3, total107/15. This trial does not claim optimality; the authentic spinner game must preserve the sequence, one-time placement decisions, four round results and the tie-break rule.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — minimize summed difference: using the same eight input digits exactly once, a first-party trial is1/2−1/3=1/6 and4/5−2/6=7/15, total19/30. Learners may choose different legal arrangements and argue whose summed differences are nearest zero. Require exact use-once checks, nonzero denominators and a declared policy if they produce a negative difference; the source allows discussion of swapping order, not blind automatic reordering.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Teacher boundary: randomly drawn digits, irreversibility of moves, four-round interaction, per-round winner, tie-break and choices to seek a small difference must be teacher-reviewed. Checking one computed fraction cannot certify the original competitive mathematical process.

KeyConcepts.Title: Difference with unlike denominators
KeyConcepts.Definition: Use equivalent fractions with common units before subtraction.
KeyConcepts.Example: Subtracting a smaller positive amount leaves a larger result.

KeyConcepts.Title: Use-once digit constraints
KeyConcepts.Definition: A legal arrangement must use all and only supplied digits in specified numerator/denominator positions.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 1,1,2,2,3,4,5,6 each occurs the required number of times.
KeyConcepts.Example: A legal result may still be a losing trial.

KeyConcepts.Title: Different objectives
KeyConcepts.Definition: Largest difference maximizes subtraction result; closest-to-zero differences minimize a chosen total or distance to zero.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Compare rational values, not just numerators.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Change a digit after the next spinner result
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The game explicitly commits each placed number and forbids changing it.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep a chronological written move record.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Accept a mathematically correct difference as a legal game submission without checking digits
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The required digit bank, available positions and turn order constrain valid plays.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Check the complete sequence and multiplicities, not only arithmetic.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat fictional spinner outcomes as the only official correct source game totals.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original IM2021 printed student activities use specific decimal values and require place-value reasoning, so substituting unrelated examples or accepting a right-justified digit alignment does not preserve source parity.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Preserve original printed warm-up and precise game constraints; evaluate actual student play by teacher rubric.
